aspects.says: Double-checked locking is correct only with a volatile field, because without it another thread can see the reference before the object is constructed.
aspects.reason: practised on 5.3.3 by 'Lazy initialization with double-checked locking'

aspects.says: Deadlock is prevented by taking locks in one fixed order, or by tryLock with a timeout.
aspects.reason: deadlock prevention is practised in the course's synchronization module (21), lesson 6.2.1

aspects.says: The initialization-on-demand holder gets lazy, thread-safe initialization from the class initialization lock, without volatile.
aspects.reason: its laziness and safety come from class loading, which a graded test cannot tell apart from an eager static field; the quiz's two questions go to the consistency guarantees

aspects.says: Lock.unlock and lock give the same edges as a monitor, and add try-lock, timed and interruptible locking and conditions.
aspects.reason: explicit locks are the subject of the course's module 22 (locks and semaphores); this page only states they share the monitor's memory semantics

aspects.says: The JVM implements volatile and monitors with memory barriers, and VarHandle exposes weaker orderings.
aspects.reason: barriers are how the JVM implements the rules, not something Java code can observe; reordering is the subject of 5.1.4

aspects.says: Lock on a dedicated, private, final object, never on a boxed value, a mutable reference or an object outside code can reach.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: The JMM is happens-before consistent, weaker than sequential consistency, but a program with no data races appears sequentially consistent.
A read-write lock lets many readers in at once but only one writer.
aspects.reason: read-write locks are the subject of the course's module 22 (locks and semaphores)

aspects.says: A monitor release gives an edge only to later acquisitions of the same monitor.
Keep slow work such as I/O outside the lock and hold it only to update shared state.
synchronized gives both atomicity and visibility to the region it protects, while volatile gives visibility only.
aspects.reason: practised in part on 5.3.3 by 'Lazy initialization with double-checked locking', whose lock makes check-and-create atomic; the volatile half of the contrast is asked on 5.1.1 by its quiz question on counters

aspects.says: wait() and await() can wake spuriously, so the condition is re-checked in a loop.
aspects.reason: wait and notify are practised in the synchronization module (21); a spurious wakeup cannot be produced on demand by a test
